metadata.description:
Monthly and weekly hydropower generation and operating constraints for 1,483 conventional hydropower plants across the contiguous United States, 1982-2024, for 11 climate ensemble members.

Each member gives, per plant and per period, predicted generation plus the four quantities production cost and capacity expansion models need to dispatch a hydro plant: minimum power, maximum power, average daily operational range (a ramping limit), and period target energy.

Produced for the U.S. Department of Energy's FORESIGHT project at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (weather extremes task, hydrology).

Read "Members, and what they can be used for" before using this dataset. The 11 members are not interchangeable, and 10 of them must not be compared against observations timestep by timestep.

Contents

Total download about 1.6 GB (327 MB monthly, 1.3 GB weekly, 250 KB metadata).

File Rows Plants Size
era5d_monthly.parquet 765,228 1,483 36 MB
era5d_weekly.parquet 3,356,967 1,473 174 MB
ic0_monthly.parquet … ic9_monthly.parquet 765,228 each 1,483 ~30 MB each
ic0_weekly.parquet … ic9_weekly.parquet 3,356,967 each 1,473 ~119 MB each
foresight_hydro_plants.csv 1,483 1,483 123 KB
foresight_hydro_plants_with_huc2.csv 1,483 1,483 126 KB

Every member covers the same plants, the same periods, and the same schema, so files can be concatenated on the scenario column. Weekly files carry 10 fewer plants than monthly; see "Known limitations".

Parquet is the only format provided. It is readable from R (arrow), Python (pandas, polars, pyarrow), DuckDB, and Spark without conversion. See "Quick start".

Data dictionary

Generation and constraint files (<member>_{monthly,weekly}.parquet)

Column Type Units Description
datetime date — First day of the period (month or week)
eia_id double — EIA plant code; join key to the metadata CSV
plant string — Plant name
power_predicted_mwh double MWh Predicted net generation over the period
n_hours double h Hours in the period; use to convert MWh to MW and back
p_avg double MW Average power over the period, power_predicted_mwh / n_hours
p_max double MW Maximum power the plant may be dispatched to
p_min double MW Minimum power the plant may be dispatched to
ador double MW Average daily operational range, a ramping limit
scenario string — Member name, one of era5d, ic0 … ic9

power_predicted_mwh is the target energy for the period. p_avg is the same quantity as a rate. Values are rounded to five decimal places.

Generation is clipped before the constraints are derived: negative predictions are set to zero and predictions above nameplate capacity are set to nameplate, so 0 <= p_avg <= nameplate_capacity holds everywhere and power_predicted_mwh is consistent with the clipped p_avg.

The constraints follow the GODEEEP-hydro formulation, with per-plant parameters in the metadata CSV:

p_max = p_avg + max_param * (nameplate_capacity - p_avg)
p_min = min_param * p_avg
ador  = ador_param * (p_max - p_min)

The parameters were fit to 28 Columbia basin federal projects with observed sub-daily operating records. Those 28 plants use their own fitted values; every other plant uses the average for its operating mode (run-of-river or storage). p_max, p_min, and ador are therefore a statistical envelope typical of plants of that mode, not a plant-specific licensed operating limit. Do not read them as regulatory or physical constraints for a named plant.

Plant metadata (foresight_hydro_plants.csv)

Column Units Description
eia_id — EIA plant code
plant — Plant name
mode — RoR (run-of-river) or Storage
state — Two-letter state code
lat, lon degrees Plant location, WGS84
nameplate_capacity MW Nameplate capacity
nerc_region — NERC region
ba — Balancing authority
max_param, min_param, ador_param — Constraint parameters, see above

foresight_hydro_plants_with_huc2.csv adds a huc2 column, the two-digit USGS hydrologic unit code (1-18) the plant falls in, for regional aggregation.

The fleet is 1,483 plants totaling 79,287 MW across 46 states, 46 balancing authorities, 6 NERC regions, and all 18 CONUS HUC2 regions: 921 storage plants (55,250 MW) and 562 run-of-river plants (24,036 MW).

Time conventions

Monthly. datetime is the first of the month. n_hours is the number of days in that month times 24. 516 months, 1982-01 through 2024-12.

Weekly. Weeks restart on January 1 of each year rather than running continuously, so week boundaries align across years and each year has exactly 53 weeks. Weeks 1 through 52 are seven days (n_hours 168); week 53 is the remainder of the calendar year, one day in a common year (n_hours 24) and two in a leap year (48). datetime is the first day of the week. 2,279 weeks, 1982-01-01 through 2024-12-30.

Because week 53 is short, sum power_predicted_mwh rather than averaging p_avg when aggregating weeks, or weight by n_hours.

Members, and what they can be used for

Member Forcing Weather aligned with history?
era5d ERA5 reanalysis, downscaled Yes
ic0 … ic9 ACE2 emulator, downscaled No

All 11 members are driven by the same river routing model (mosartwmpy) over the same 1980-2024 period, and all 11 use one set of regression coefficients fit on era5d. What differs is the weather that drove the routing.

era5d is the reference member

era5d is driven by downscaled ERA5 reanalysis, so its weather sequence follows what actually happened. It is the only member that can be compared against an observed generation record or a stream gauge timestep by timestep, and the only member the regression is trained on.

Use era5d for any paired comparison against observations, as a historical reconstruction, and as the reference case the ensemble statistics are measured against.

The one thing not to do with era5d is pool it into the ensemble. It is a single reanalysis-driven run, not a draw from the same stochastic process as ic0 … ic9, so it does not belong in a distribution, a quantile, or a member-mean computed over the ACE2 members.

Note that era5d is predicted in-sample. From 2002 on, where the observed generation record exists, its predictions use observed generation as the lagged generation predictor, so agreement with observations over those years is not an out-of-sample result. Before 2002 it uses the model without generation lags. The honest skill estimate is the drop-one-year cross validation under "Validation", not a direct comparison of era5d against the record it was fit on.

ic0 … ic9 are an ensemble, not 10 histories

The ic members come from the ACE2 downscaled ensemble, which produces stochastic emulator realizations rather than reanalysis-constrained weather. They span 1982-2024 and reproduce the climate and the seasonal cycle of that period, but their weather sequence is a plausible alternative to the observed one, not the observed one.

Correlating routed outflow against era5d at three major gauges, with the seasonal cycle removed so only weather variability remains:

Gauge Monthly anomaly r vs era5d Water-year r vs era5d
The Dalles (14105700) 0.35 0.40
Below Hoover (09421500) 0.33 0.53
Priest Rapids (12472800) 0.28 0.29

A weather-aligned run scores far higher on the same test: a Livneh-forced simulation reaches 0.76, 0.54, and 0.71 on the monthly anomaly test and 0.84, 0.81, and 0.69 on the water-year test at these gauges.

Valid uses. Treat ic0 … ic9 as 10 samples from the distribution of hydropower conditions consistent with the recent climate: return periods, drought duration and severity statistics, the spread of annual and seasonal generation, tail risk, and the correlation structure across plants and regions within a member. The ensemble exists to supply more samples of plausible weather than the single observed record contains.

Invalid uses. Do not read an ic member as a reconstruction of a particular year — ic3 in 1997 is not the 1997 that happened. Do not compare an ic member against an observed timeseries timestep by timestep. Do not average across members expecting to recover the observed record; averaging 10 unsynchronized realizations suppresses exactly the variability that makes them useful.

In one sentence: the ensemble supports distributional and climatological inference, and era5d supports event-by-event comparison against observations.

How the dataset was produced

The method is GODEEEP-hydro's, unchanged, and is documented in full in Bracken et al., Scientific Data (2025). In outline:

  1. Routing. mosartwmpy routes gridded runoff through the river network and reservoir operations, producing daily channel inflow, channel outflow, and reservoir storage per grid cell. Eleven runs were made, one per member.
  2. Extraction. For each plant, the three variables are taken from the grid cell nearest the dam.
  3. Regression. For each plant, a linear model predicts generation from lagged flow and storage — 12 monthly or 53 weekly lags of square-root outflow, inflow, square-root storage, and generation. Models are fit on era5d against observed generation, using RectifHyd 1.4 as the target and observed daily records for the Columbia basin federal projects. Two models are fit per plant, one with lagged generation terms and one without, for periods before the observed generation record begins.
  4. Prediction. era5d is predicted directly. Each ic member is stepped forward one period at a time, feeding each prediction back in as the generation lag, because generation is autoregressive in this model.
  5. Constraints. The Columbia basin parameters are applied to derive p_min, p_max, and ador as described above.

Lag construction consumes the first two years of routing output: 1980 supplies the lags for 1981, and 1981 is then dropped so the autoregressive recursion starts from a complete year. That is why the routing covers 1980-2024 while the dataset starts in 1982.

Because all 11 members share one set of coefficients, a plant that era5d fits poorly is fit poorly in all 11 members, and the skill statistics below describe the era5d fit rather than any ic member's skill.

Validation

Full validation, including the figures and the tests behind these numbers, is in the validation report distributed with this release (report.html, a self-contained interactive document). Headline results:

Cross validation. Drop-one-year cross validation of the reference member (era5d) against its observed generation record, over all plants:

Timescale Plants Median KGE Median r
Monthly 1,483 0.806 0.832
Weekly 1,472 0.779 0.810

The lagged-predictor formulation is what buys this. The same cross validation of the original hydrofixr model — a single-predictor regression on contemporaneous outflow — gives median KGE 0.407 monthly and 0.316 weekly on the same plants.

Columbia basin federal projects, against observed daily generation for 28 projects, aggregated:

Timescale Projects Median KGE Range
Monthly 28 0.783 0.590 - 0.897
Weekly 28 0.778 0.594 - 0.866

Against the predecessor dataset. era5d reproduces GODEEEP-hydro 1.2's historical run over the 1982-2013 window the two share, despite a different routing simulation: plant-level annual generation r 0.998, CONUS annual total r 0.976, CONUS monthly anomaly r 0.955, and mean CONUS generation within 0.3% (275.9 against 275.1 TWh/yr). Per-plant annual correlation has a median of 0.871 (IQR 0.797-0.922), so the fleet is unmoved in aggregate while individual plants shift.

Ensemble behavior. Every ic member shows the designed signature — the same climate as the reference member, independent weather. Correlations are against era5d over 1982-2024:

Member Seasonal r Annual r Monthly anomaly r Mean TWh/yr Interannual sd TWh 1982-91 → 2015-24
era5d — — — 274.1 22.3 280.8 → 269.8
ic0 0.985 +0.054 +0.066 285.2 22.6 287.4 → 278.4
ic1 0.994 +0.206 +0.130 286.8 18.1 295.2 → 285.3
ic2 0.992 +0.086 +0.092 282.2 25.5 293.3 → 270.0
ic3 0.993 +0.206 +0.163 282.8 20.9 292.1 → 263.2
ic4 0.993 +0.088 +0.048 281.6 17.3 290.7 → 274.9
ic5 0.993 +0.498 +0.383 282.6 22.1 299.6 → 276.4
ic6 0.996 +0.214 +0.176 280.2 17.2 285.8 → 278.7
ic7 0.992 +0.032 +0.039 280.7 17.6 285.5 → 278.3
ic8 0.990 +0.347 +0.247 281.6 22.6 300.0 → 266.2
ic9 0.996 -0.063 +0.010 287.4 16.5 280.3 → 284.7

Seasonal correlation is 0.985 or better for every member while annual correlation stays low and unsigned. That contrast is the intended design, not a defect: it is what "right climate, different weather" looks like in the output. Members run 2.2% to 4.8% above era5d in the mean, a known positive offset, and all decline over the period except ic9.

Known limitations

Conduit and aqueduct plants are not well represented. Their generation follows managed water deliveries — city supply, canal schedules, pumped storage cycles — which the river routing does not simulate, so the routed flow at their grid cells carries little signal. Seven Los Angeles basin plants, all under 11 MW, had weekly cross-validated KGE below -1 and are excluded from the weekly files: Venice (72), Sepulveda Canyon (316), Foothill (396), Franklin (397), San Fernando (403), Azusa (6449), and Sawtelle (7077). They remain in the monthly files, where aggregation largely recovers them. Three more plants with known-bad weekly observed data are also excluded from the weekly files: 7224, 7229, and 7372. Borderline conduit plants (San Francisquito 1 and 2, San Gabriel, Castaic, Moccasin) are retained in both. This accounts for the difference between 1,483 monthly plants and 1,473 weekly.

Missing values. era5d_weekly.parquet contains 56 rows with power_predicted_mwh null, all at Pilot Butte (EIA 674). Three weeks of that plant's observed 2022 generation are missing, and because the model uses 53 weekly lags of generation, each gap blanks every later week that lags across it. This is the only null in the release: the other 21 files contain none, and no file contains a negative or non-finite generation value. Only the trained member uses observed generation lags, so no ic member is affected. Code consuming era5d_weekly.parquet should handle nulls rather than assume completeness.

Constraints are mode averages, not plant limits. See the note under the data dictionary. Only the 28 Columbia basin federal projects have plant-specific parameters.

Skill is inherited, not per member. The cross-validation statistics describe the era5d fit. They are the right guide to which plants are modeled well, and they say nothing about how closely an ic member tracks any particular year.

Quick start

DuckDB, no setup, straight from the files:

-- CONUS monthly generation for every member
SELECT scenario, datetime, sum(power_predicted_mwh) / 1e6 AS twh
FROM read_parquet('*_monthly.parquet')
GROUP BY scenario, datetime
ORDER BY datetime, scenario;

R:

library(arrow)
library(dplyr)

plants <- readr::read_csv("foresight_hydro_plants.csv")

# one plant, monthly, across the whole ensemble
grand_coulee <- open_dataset(list.files(pattern = "_monthly[.]parquet$")) |>
  filter(eia_id == 6163) |>
  collect()

# annual generation by member
annual <- open_dataset(list.files(pattern = "_monthly[.]parquet$")) |>
  group_by(scenario, year = lubridate::year(datetime)) |>
  summarise(twh = sum(power_predicted_mwh) / 1e6) |>
  collect()

Python:

import pandas as pd

era5d = pd.read_parquet("era5d_monthly.parquet")
plants = pd.read_csv("foresight_hydro_plants.csv")

df = era5d.merge(plants, on="eia_id")
df["capacity_factor"] = df["p_avg"] / df["nameplate_capacity"]

# ensemble spread in annual CONUS generation
import glob
ens = pd.concat(pd.read_parquet(f) for f in glob.glob("ic?_monthly.parquet"))
ens["year"] = ens["datetime"].dt.year
annual = (ens.groupby(["scenario", "year"])["power_predicted_mwh"]
             .sum().div(1e6).rename("twh").reset_index())
print(annual.groupby("year")["twh"].describe()[["min", "50%", "max"]])

The weekly files are large enough that a column and row filter pushed into the Parquet reader (open_dataset in R, pyarrow.dataset or read_parquet(columns=, filters=) in Python, DuckDB in all cases) is much faster than reading a whole file into memory.

Citation

Cite the dataset and the method paper.

Dataset:

Bracken, C. (2026). FORESIGHT-hydro 1.0.0: monthly and weekly hydropower generation and operating constraints for CONUS plants, 1982-2024, for an 11-member climate ensemble [Data set]. <DOI to be assigned at publication>

Method:

Bracken, C., Son, Y., Broman, D., & Voisin, N. (2025). GODEEEP-hydro: Historical and projected power system ready hydropower data for the United States. Scientific Data, 12, 875. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-025-05097-3

Provenance and related datasets

  • Predecessor. GODEEEP-hydro 1.0 and 1.1, https://zenodo.org/records/14269763. This dataset uses the same method and, for the trained member, reproduces GODEEEP-hydro 1.2's historical run over the years they share.
  • Training target. RectifHyd 1.4, plant-level reconciled monthly and weekly generation.
  • Independent observational reference. RectifHydPlus 1.1 (Turner et al. 2025), used in the validation report as a check the pipeline never trains on.
  • Plant metadata. ORNL Existing Hydropower Assets database, FY2023 revision.
  • Routing model. mosartwmpy, https://github.com/IMMM-SFA/mosartwmpy.
  • Code. The full pipeline that produced this dataset is in the FORESIGHT-hydro repository, a fork of GODEEEP-hydro 1.2.

The mosartwmpy routing simulations were produced by collaborators on the FORESIGHT weather extremes task.
